title: Breakdown of material-time scaling in the microscopic dynamics of metallic glasses
authors: Till Böhmer, Jie Shen, Jan Philipp Gabriel, Rolf Zeißler, Federico Zontone, Fan Yang, Eloi Pineda, Beatrice Ruta, Thomas Blochowicz
abstract: Physical aging in glasses is often described using the concept of material time, which assumes the underlying relaxation mechanism to remain the same as in equilibrium, but with a rate that changes during aging. Whether material time also captures the microscopic dynamics of metallic glasses, which differ qualitatively between the glass and the equilibrium supercooled liquid, is unclear. Using simultaneous time-resolved X-ray diffraction and X-ray photon-correlation spectroscopy, we follow the full equilibration of a metallic glass after small temperature jumps starting from equilibrium. The time evolution of the first sharp diffraction peak position exhibits the asymmetry between temperature up- and down-jumps characteristic of material-time aging and is quantitatively described by the Tool-Narayanaswamy-Moynihan model, which is based on this concept. By contrast, the microscopic density-density autocorrelation functions strongly violate material-time scaling. Compressed-exponential relaxation emerges even after temperature changes as small as 4K, irrespective of the direction of the temperature jump, and continuously evolves into a stretched-exponential relaxation shape following the equilibration of the average structure. This behavior is consistent with a transient stress-mediated contribution associated with volumetric frustration that disappears upon equilibration. Our results show that a material time can describe the evolution of average structural properties even when the corresponding microscopic dynamics do not obey material-time scaling.
summary: This experimental study uses X-ray scattering to probe aging in metallic glasses, comparing macroscopic structural changes to microscopic dynamics. While the average structure follows predictions based on 'material time,' the underlying microscopic correlations violate this scaling. The findings suggest that material time is an effective description for average structure but fails to capture the full complexity of the microscopic relaxation processes.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the concept of 'material time,' used to describe physical aging in glasses, accurately captures the underlying microscopic dynamics of metallic glasses.
main_result: The average structural properties follow material-time scaling, but the microscopic density-density correlations strongly violate this scaling, suggesting the two descriptions are decoupled.
method: The study uses simultaneous time-resolved X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray photon-correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) following small temperature jumps.
model_or_system: The system studied is a metallic glass (MG), specifically $	ext{Zr}_{46.8}	ext{Ti}_{8.2}	ext{Cu}_{7.5}	ext{Ni}_{10}	ext{Be}_{27.5}$. The analysis compares macroscopic structural evolution (modeled by TNM) against microscopic dynamics.
key_observables: First sharp diffraction peak position ($q_{	ext{FSDP}}$), two-time intensity autocorrelation function ($g_2(t_1, t_2)$), and the violation of the triangular relation.
important_parameters: Temperature jump magnitude ($\Delta T$), relaxation exponents ($ eta$), and the material time parameter ($\xi$).
main_assumptions: The TNM model assumes a specific form for the relaxation kernel, and the analysis tests the validity of the material-time scaling hypothesis.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of the autocorrelation function shape (from compressed-exponential to stretched-exponential) and test the triangular relation, showing systematic violations during aging.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the structural evolution consistent with material-time aging (TNM model) using XRD. It then probes the microscopic dynamics using XPCS, demonstrating that these correlations violate the material-time scaling criteria, leading to the conclusion that the two descriptions are distinct.
why_interesting: The decoupling of macroscopic structural relaxation from microscopic dynamics provides a nuanced view of aging, suggesting that simple time reparameterizations may only capture average structural changes, not the full quantum mechanical relaxation pathways.

FIG. 2. Test of the triangular relation for two-time autocorrelation functions during aging after (a) a temperature down-jump from 615 K to 600 K and (b) an up-jump from 595 K to 607 K. The correlation C13 is plotted as a function of C12 for three fixed values of C23 = 1.009, 1.013, and 1.018. Colors indicate the waiting time t1 after the temperature jump. For a valid material-time description, C13 should be uniquely determined by C12 and C23 and therefore independent of t1. The systematic dependence on t1 observed for both temperature jumps demonstrates a violation of the triangular relation.

FIG. 3. Aging of the average structure following temperature up- and down-jumps. (a) Evolution of the FSDP position qFSDP relative to its equilibrium value at the final temper- ature, plotted as a function of time normalized by the av- erage equilibrium relaxation time ⟨τ(T∞)⟩. (b) Normalized structural relaxation R(t) for the largest down- and up-jumps. Solid black lines show the corresponding TNM predictions us- ing a common parameter set. The inset shows the evolution of ∆qFSDP(t) around t = 0, including the TNM prediction dur- ing the finite-duration temperature jump before T∞is reached (t < 0).

FIG. 4. Evolution of the deviation from equilibrium of the FSDP maximum, |qFSDP(t)−qeq FSDP(T∞)| (red, left axes), and the KWW stretching exponent β(t) (blue, right axes) during aging after (a) a temperature down-jump from 615 K to 600 K and (b) an up-jump from 595 K to 607 K.
